one_liner: Code generator for FIX SBE fixed-layout binary messages; C++ flyweight codecs beat Protobuf ~9x encode, ~7x decode (one small-message test).
what_it_does: This is the reference implementation of the FIX Trading Community's Simple Binary Encoding. You describe messages in an SBE XML schema, and a Java tool (the sbe-all jar) generates codecs for C++, C, Java, C#, Go and Rust. The C++ output is a set of generated headers with flyweight classes that you wrap over your own char buffer. To write, you call wrapAndApplyHeader or wrapForEncode, set fields with fluent setters, set a group count and call next() per entry, and put length-prefixed var data last. To read, you wrap a MessageHeader and then call wrapForDecode with its block length and version. It is not a drop-in for Protobuf: the IDL, the wire format and the API are all different. If you want owning objects, an optional generator flag (sbe.cpp.generate.dtos) emits C++17 DTOs with encodeWith/decodeWith.
how_it_is_fast: Every field has a fixed offset inside its root or group block. A getter or setter therefore compiles to a memcpy of a native-width value at buffer + constant offset, plus a __builtin_bswap only when the schema byte order differs from the host. There is no varint coding, tag dispatch or presence bookkeeping. The flyweight pattern reads and writes the caller's buffer directly, with no intermediate message object, heap allocation or extra copy; the project's Design Principles call these 'copy-free', 'allocation-free' and 'native type mapping'. Access is strictly ascending and sequential, so the codec tracks one position cursor, and the only per-advance cost is a __builtin_expect-hinted bounds compare, which SBE_NO_BOUNDS_CHECK compiles out.
when_to_use: Low-latency trading or messaging paths (market data, order entry, Aeron transport) where messages are mostly fixed-width numbers, enums and short fixed char arrays, and both ends share one SBE schema, for example an exchange feed published as SBE XML.
Hot paths that must not allocate: encoding straight into a preallocated send or ring buffer, and decoding in place from the receive buffer.
Small messages (tens to a few hundred bytes), where Protobuf's per-message object construction and varint parsing dominate. The measured case was a 138-byte message with 3 repeating-group entries.
Polyglot systems that need the same wire format from C++, C, Java, C#, Go and Rust, all generated from one schema.
Consumers that read each message once, front to back (streaming decode), rather than looking fields up at random.
when_not_to_use: Schemas that change often or need fields removed, changed or reordered. Only adding fields at the end of a block (with sinceVersion, presence=optional) stays backward-compatible, and composites cannot gain fields without a new message template and schema version.

Sparse or mostly-optional data. Optional fields still take their full fixed width and use in-band null sentinels, and fixed-length char arrays are padded. The cited test encoded to 138 bytes vs Protobuf's 120.

Random access or partial reads of large nested documents. The FAQ says you cannot randomly access fields. Groups and var data must be walked, or explicitly skipped, in schema order to reach whatever follows them.

Parsing untrusted input with only the built-in checks. Open issue #969 (since 2024-01) reports that a received group blockLength is not validated against the fields being read, so a crafted small blockLength lets field reads run past the buffer.

Builds that cannot run a JVM at codegen time or must use -fno-exceptions. The generator is a Java 17 jar, and generated code throws std::runtime_error, e.g. for group index overrun or an unknown enum value, even with bounds checks off.

integration.form: header-only (headers generated per schema by the Java sbe-all jar; the optional on-the-fly (OTF) decoder is a header-only CMake INTERFACE target)
integration.dependencies: Generated C++ codecs: C++ standard library only. Code generation: Java 17+ runtime to run sbe-all (the 'all' jar bundles Agrona). Building this repo: CMake 3.30+ and Gradle.
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 for generated codecs; C++17 adds std::string_view accessors and [[nodiscard]], and C++20 adds std::span overloads. DTOs require C++17. CI builds with GCC 11-14 and Clang 17-22 on Ubuntu 24.04, Xcode clang on macOS 15, and MSVC on windows-latest.
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows per the README. Any CPU where __BYTE_ORDER__ is defined (GCC/Clang) or WIN32 is set; the generated header #errors otherwise. Big- and little-endian hosts are both handled via byte swaps. The cited benchmark ran on aarch64 (Apple M1 Pro).
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Flyweights are mutable cursors (buffer pointer, offset, position) with no locking, so give each thread its own encoder/decoder instance.

gotchas: Access order is a contract that is not checked by default. Groups and var data must be encoded and decoded in schema order and skipped explicitly, with next() called per group element. Violations silently produce invalid messages or misreads. Runtime checks need codegen with -Dsbe.generate.precedence.checks=true plus compiling with SBE_ENABLE_PRECEDENCE_CHECKS, and the wiki warns of significant overhead.

Bounds checks are on by default and throw std::runtime_error (e.g. 'buffer too short [E100]'). SBE's own sbe-benchmarks define SBE_NO_BOUNDS_CHECK in Release builds, so compare numbers only at the same setting.
Decoded values are views into the buffer; copy anything you keep after the buffer is reused. getXAsString() allocates a std::string, while getXAsStringView() (C++17) does not.

Older-version reads return in-band null sentinels for fields past the acting block length, e.g. the minimum value for signed integers and the maximum for unsigned. Test xInActingVersion() rather than comparing values.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick SBE over YaFF, ProtoCache or Apache Fory when you need a standardized (FIX), cross-language, fixed-layout wire format that is written in place into your own buffer with no allocation, as in market-data and order gateways. The siblings report their wins over Protobuf mostly on read, decode-and-traverse or throughput benchmarks; prefer them when your data is nested or optional-heavy and not consumed strictly in order, where SBE's fixed layout and sequential-access rule fit poorly.
verified_claims_summary: chronoxor/CppSerialization is a 167-star suite by the author of FastBinaryEncoding. In it, converting a 128-byte Account with 3 Orders from plain C++ structs and back took 35 ns to encode and 52 ns to decode with SBE, vs 322/351 ns for Protobuf (a fresh message with no arena, SerializeToString/ParseFromString). The run was on an Apple M1 Pro (macOS, 'release' configuration); the build scripts set C++23 but the compiler and flags are unstated, and Protobuf was an unpinned main-branch build. The reports are dated 2025-07-16, when the suite vendored sbe-all-1.35.6.jar; the 1.40.1 jar was only added on 2026-09-09. The suite does not define SBE_NO_BOUNDS_CHECK, so SBE's default bounds checks were presumably on.
status_note: Actively maintained by Real Logic/Aeron (1.40.2 released and last commit on 2026-09-17, 3.5k stars) under Apache-2.0. The C++ side is just generated headers, so it is easy to adopt as long as you can run the Java generator in your build.
